Distinct labels preclude nonidentity rotational stabilizers.

routes.label: Count crossings of the triangular wave

audits.mathematicalReason: Since 0≤f≤1, every solution satisfies 0<x≤n; x=n is a solution. Put g(x)=xf(x). For x<n, the outer equation is equivalent to g(x)±x/(2n)=k+1/2 for integers k≥0. On [j,j+1/2], g(x)=(2j+1)x−2x², and on [j+1/2,j+1], g(x)=2x²−(2j+1)x. Counting half-integer level crossings of these quadratic branches gives 4j+2 distinct solutions in each unit interval, j=0,...,n−1. The first small arch crosses no such level; at x=n the two branch descriptions represent one solution and must be merged. Thus the total is sum(4j+2)=2n². Since 2·31²=1922<2012≤2048=2·32², the minimum is 32. Both proposed routes support this exact branch-and-endpoint count.

Factoring gives (x−b)(2x−a−c)=0, so the root sum is b+(a+c)/2=(a+b+c+b)/2. Distinct one-digit numbers satisfy a+b+c≤9+8+7=24 and b≤9. Hence the sum is at most (24+9)/2=16.5, attained by b=9 and {a,c}={7,8}. Expansion followed by the quadratic root-sum relation gives the same expression, so both routes are valid.

Reflection sends (x,y) to (16−x,y), producing vertices (10,5), (8,−3), and (7,1). Each triangle has area 8. Their upper sloping sides intersect at T=(8,7/3), and their overlap is the quadrilateral with vertices (8,−3), (9,1), T, and (7,1). Splitting it along the horizontal segment from (7,1) to (9,1) gives area 4+4/3=16/3. Therefore the union has area 16−16/3=32/3. Alternatively, the ordered concave union boundary (6,5), (8,−3), (10,5), T gives the same area by shoelace. Both listed routes are defensible.

Every interior angle is 120°. The law of cosines gives AC²=CE²=EA²=r²+r+1, so triangle ACE is equilateral with area sqrt(3)(r²+r+1)/4. Each of the three removed corner triangles has area r·sqrt(3)/4. Thus the hexagon's area is sqrt(3)(r²+4r+1)/4. The ratio condition gives 10(r²+r+1)=7(r²+4r+1), or r²−6r+1=0. Its roots are 3±2sqrt(2), both positive and geometrically admissible, and their sum is 6. Vieta is a valid selected method for this sum; coordinates and shoelace provide an alternative area calculation.

routes.label: Locate contact points and compute area
Subtract areas from the centers' triangle

audits.mathematicalReason: External tangency gives center distances 3,4,5, so the centers form a right triangle. Place the radius-1 center at (0,0), the radius-2 center at (3,0), and the radius-3 center at (0,4). The contact points are (1,0), (0,1), and (9/5,8/5), whose coordinate area is 6/5. Alternatively, subtract corner areas 1/2, 8/5, and 27/10 from the centers' triangle area 6. In that route, similarity applies to auxiliary right triangles formed by perpendicular projections to obtain heights; it does not require the corner triangles themselves to be similar to the centers' triangle.

Since tan A=BC/AC=3/4, write BC=3t and AC=4t with t>0. Pythagoras gives AB=5t. The perimeter is 12t=36, so t=3 and AB=15. This is a valid right-triangle solution using the tangent definition and Pythagorean theorem.

A permissible number of students per row is exactly a positive divisor of the total N. Twelve different layouts followed by no new layout mean N has exactly twelve positive divisors. The specified layouts require 15|N and 6|N, hence 30|N. The only positive multiple of 30 below 60 is 30, which has eight divisors. But 60=2²·3·5 has (2+1)(1+1)(1+1)=12 divisors and permits both specified layouts. Thus 60 is minimal. Either direct divisor enumeration or the prime-exponent formula establishes the required count.

With T teams, every game corresponds to one unordered pair, so T(T−1)/2=21. Equivalently, counting team appearances gives T(T−1)=42 because each game contributes two appearances. The equation factors as (T−7)(T+6)=0; the positive feasible solution is T=7. Both proposed counting routes are valid, and unordered selection supports the combinations concept.

Logarithm laws and the exponential-logarithm inverse give e^p=product(k^k), for k=1 through 6. Only 2², 4⁴, and 6⁶ contribute factors of 2, with exponents 2, 8, and 6. Therefore v₂(e^p)=16, and the largest power of 2 dividing it is 2^16. The assessed scope explicitly includes tracking prime exponents in products, so its use here is defensible even though no factorial formula is needed.
